architectureLayers.label: Federal product safety
architectureLayers.body: 49 U.S.C. Chapter 301, FMVSS, certification, exemptions, defects and recalls.

architectureLayers.label: California road use
architectureLayers.body: DMV permits for drivered testing, driverless testing and deployment.

architectureLayers.label: California passenger service
architectureLayers.body: CPUC pilot/deployment authority, safety plans, fare rules and reporting.

profiles.architectureConclusion: A vehicle may satisfy the federal product layer and still lack California road-use or passenger-service authority.

sections.title: Product compliance is federal; road permission is not
paragraphs: NHTSA administers the Motor Vehicle Safety Act and FMVSS. The federal model generally relies on manufacturer certification, together with defect, recall and enforcement powers.

A temporary exemption under 49 CFR Part 555 may be relevant where a design does not comply with an applicable standard. Neither certification nor an exemption authorises driverless operation on California public roads.
sections.takeaway: Federal product-safety compliance and state road-use permission answer different legal questions.

sections.title: Testing and deployment follow separate DMV permit stages
paragraphs: California regulates testing and deployment through distinct DMV permit categories: testing with a safety driver, driverless testing and deployment.
The 2026 rules strengthen safety-case, remote-operations, first-responder, reporting and enforcement requirements. Use the adopted Articles 3.7 and 3.8, not historic proposals.
sections.takeaway: California has a real deployment route, but it is conditional, phased and permit-based.

sections.title: DMV deployment permission is not passenger-service authority
paragraphs: The California Public Utilities Commission regulates AV passenger service. Pilot and deployment programmes differ on fare collection and require the relevant DMV permit.
Compensated passenger service therefore requires analysis of both the DMV road-use layer and CPUC operating authority, safety-plan and reporting requirements.
sections.takeaway: DMV controls AV road access; CPUC separately controls passenger-service authority.

sections.title: Remote driver and remote assistant are not interchangeable
paragraphs: California's current regulations distinguish remote driving from remote assistance. The role's legal significance depends on whether the person performs driving functions or provides non-driving support.
Atlas must not flatten every person outside the vehicle into a generic remote operator.
sections.takeaway: The correct question is which legal and operational function the remote human performs.

sections.title: The approved operating model can be narrowed by permit conditions
paragraphs: California DMV can impose restrictions relating to location, speed, weather, fleet size and other safety-relevant conditions. CPUC permit records may separately identify a passenger-service ODD.
This is not a standalone Germany-style operating-area approval. The legally relevant scope emerges from the safety case, DMV permit and any CPUC conditions.
sections.takeaway: ODD is both a safety-evidence boundary and an operating constraint, but California's legal mechanism is permit-based.

sections.title: Safety assurance continues after the permit is granted
paragraphs: California combines phased testing, a structured safety case, first-responder plans, remote-operations requirements, reporting and targeted enforcement.
Federal defect oversight and NHTSA crash reporting continue after vehicles enter real-world service.
sections.takeaway: A permit is not the end of the safety process.

sections.title: Reporting obligations come from multiple authorities
paragraphs: California requires collision and operational reporting under its AV framework. NHTSA separately requires named entities to report specified ADS crashes.
NHTSA expressly cautions that public crash data are not exposure-normalised and should not be treated as simple safety rankings.
sections.takeaway: Federal and state reporting duties overlap but are not one universal incident regime.

sections.title: The permitting system does not replace general civil liability
paragraphs: California imposes an AV-specific financial-responsibility requirement, while passenger-service authority may add carrier obligations.
The reviewed AV-specific sources do not create one comprehensive federal-plus-California allocation among owner, manufacturer, ADS developer and remote personnel.
sections.takeaway: California adapts entry and financial-responsibility rules without creating a single nationwide AV liability code.

deploymentConclusion: The United States cannot be reduced to a single yes/no answer because federal and state authorities regulate different layers.
For this scenario, California provides a conditional path: federal compliance or exemption, California DMV deployment permission, and CPUC authority for compensated passenger service.
The Atlas status must therefore remain visibly California-specific.
practicalQuestions: Which FMVSS apply, and is a Part 555 exemption needed?
Which DMV permit phase applies, and what safety-case/ODD evidence is required?
Does the service require CPUC pilot or deployment authority?
Which remote human role is used: remote driver, remote assistant or another operations role?
Which federal, DMV and CPUC reporting streams apply after launch?

architectureLayers.body: Federal Law No. 258-FZ defines how experimental regimes are created and supervised.

sections.title: The legal route is an experimental legal regime
paragraphs: Federal Law No. 258-FZ creates the mechanism for experimental legal regimes. Government Resolution No. 2495 establishes the passenger VATS programme.
Participation, vehicles, territories and operating conditions are defined by the EPR. It is not a permanent nationwide AV deployment code.
sections.takeaway: Russia's current passenger VATS route is legally operational, but only inside an experimental regime.

sections.title: Category 1 and Category 2 encode different human architectures
paragraphs: A Category 1 VATS retains a test driver inside the vehicle. A Category 2 VATS operates without a driver or test driver in the cabin and uses a remote operator for monitoring and defined support.
These are source-native programme categories. Do not substitute SAE levels or use Category 2 as a universal synonym for Level 4.
sections.takeaway: Category 2 means no person in the cabin under the EPR; it does not mean unrestricted national driverless operation.

sections.title: Participant, vehicle and safety documentation must align
paragraphs: The route combines EPR participant status, a safety declaration, an accredited laboratory's conformity conclusion, registration records and programme conditions.
No single document replaces the others. This is a system-level admission architecture rather than product certification alone.
sections.takeaway: Technical conformity does not itself create public-road permission outside the EPR.

sections.title: The operator supports and monitors; the operator does not remotely drive
paragraphs: For Category 2 VATS, the operator monitors vehicle/system status, manages routing or dispatch and may activate or deactivate the automated function within programme rules.
The automated control system performs the driving task. Calling the operator a remote driver would erase a legally important distinction.
sections.takeaway: Operator ≠ remote driver.

sections.title: Technical environment and legal zone are distinct
paragraphs: The programme uses the terms 'среда штатной эксплуатации' and 'зона эксплуатации'. The first describes intended operating conditions; the second is the legally relevant territorial scope.
Atlas may relate both to the operating-domain question, but neither should be relabelled as a literal statutory ODD.
sections.takeaway: Technical capability, approved zone and EPR geography are connected but not interchangeable.

sections.title: The automated system must comply with road rules
paragraphs: The EPR requires the automated control system to comply with Russian traffic rules and includes minimum-risk behaviour, cybersecurity, functional and communication requirements.
The programme also adapts police interaction and incident procedures to the absence of a conventional in-vehicle driver.
sections.takeaway: The EPR does not suspend road rules; it reallocates how compliance and roadside interaction are achieved.

sections.title: Recording and response are built into the EPR
paragraphs: The programme requires event/video recording and duties concerning emergency notification, representative attendance and provision of relevant data.
These are EPR-specific duties, not evidence of a universal reporting regime for every automated vehicle outside the programme.
sections.takeaway: Incident response is part of the operational-authorisation architecture.

sections.title: Current allocation is experimental and role-specific
paragraphs: The programme includes responsibility and insurance provisions linked to EPR roles and requires at least RUB 10 million cover per VATS.
The proposed permanent federal law would introduce a broader allocation, but it must remain in Implementation Watch until enacted and effective.
sections.takeaway: Current EPR liability must not be replaced by the allocation proposed for future law.

sections.title: A permanent federal framework is being developed
paragraphs: In January 2026 the Ministry of Transport announced a draft intended to move VATS operation from experimental regimes toward a general public-road framework.
It addresses admission, remote support, insurance and duties, but remains proposed law.
sections.takeaway: The current answer remains EPR-only until a permanent framework is enacted and takes effect.

deploymentConclusion: Russia's current architecture is detailed for an experimental regime: vehicle categories, remote operator, safety evidence, zones, data and incident duties are defined.
Its limitation is equally important: the route applies only through the EPR and cannot be presented as general nationwide permission.
The proposed permanent federal law belongs in Implementation Watch.
practicalQuestions: Is the applicant an approved EPR participant for the selected scenario?
Does the vehicle satisfy Category 2 safety-declaration and conformity requirements?
Which operating zone and ordinary operating environment apply?
How will continuous operator monitoring and staged fleet supervision be implemented?
Which incident, data and insurance duties apply?

architectureLayers.label: Current vehicle/pilot route
architectureLayers.body: Vehicle approval and registration, VSO, self-driving listing and pilot assessment.

architectureLayers.label: Passenger-service route
architectureLayers.body: APS permit and applicable local authority/transport body consent.

profiles.architectureConclusion: Great Britain has an operational pilot pathway now, but the comprehensive 2024 Act framework is not yet fully in force.

sections.title: Great Britain is operating through a transitional pilot architecture
paragraphs: The Automated Vehicles Act 2024 establishes a comprehensive future authorisation, in-use regulation and responsibility framework. Most of that framework is subject to staged commencement and must not be presented as fully operational.

In 2026, no-safety-driver pilot deployments use a transitional route built from vehicle approval/registration, a Vehicle Special Order, listing and, where passengers are carried, an Automated Passenger Service permit.
sections.takeaway: Current pilot law and the future full AV Act framework are separate legal layers.

sections.title: The pilot permits operation without a safety driver
paragraphs: The pilot applies in England, Scotland and Wales and is distinct from trialling under the code-of-practice route, which requires a safety driver.
Assessment covers the vehicle, ADS capability, cybersecurity/software updates, operational management and passenger service where relevant.
sections.takeaway: No-safety-driver operation is possible through the pilot route, not through unrestricted general authorisation.

sections.title: The route uses several connected legal steps
paragraphs: The applicant must identify a vehicle approval route and secure registration. A Vehicle Special Order addresses relevant legal departures, while listing supports the legal and insurance treatment of the vehicle.
The official listing page currently states that no self-driving vehicles are listed. This is a dated operational fact, not evidence that listing is unavailable.
sections.takeaway: Vehicle approval, VSO, listing and road operation are distinct gates.

sections.title: Commercial passenger service requires an APS permit
paragraphs: The APS Permits Regulations 2026 create a bespoke route for passenger services using automated vehicle technology. The scheme sits alongside the pilot vehicle route and includes local consent and service obligations.
A VSO or listing is not an APS permit, and an APS permit does not replace vehicle approval.
sections.takeaway: Passenger-service permission is a separate regulatory layer.

sections.title: No safety driver does not mean no operating organisation
paragraphs: The pilot is designed for operation without a safety driver ready to perform immediate safety-critical intervention. Remote assistance and operational support may still form part of the assessed system.
Future AV Act roles such as ASDE and NUiC operator belong to future-law context until the relevant framework is commenced.
sections.takeaway: Current pilot roles and future AV Act responsibility roles must not be mixed.

sections.title: The legal scope emerges from pilot approvals and service conditions
paragraphs: ADS capability and intended operating conditions form part of the pilot evidence. VSO, listing and APS/local consent can define where and how the service operates.
Great Britain does not currently use Germany's Betriebsbereich concept. Preserve the mechanism rather than normalising every geographic restriction into one label.
sections.takeaway: The operating scope is approval- and permit-defined.

sections.title: Ordinary road law remains the baseline
paragraphs: The pilot does not create a wholesale replacement for ordinary road law. Targeted departures are managed through the Vehicle Special Order and operating conditions.
The future Statement of Safety Principles will guide full AV Act authorisation and monitoring, but the September 2026 document remains a draft under consultation.
sections.takeaway: Draft future safety principles must not be shown as current binding authorisation criteria.

sections.title: Pilot operation requires continuing evidence and reporting
paragraphs: Applicants must address incident management, reporting, cybersecurity/software updating and continued safe operation. APS permit holders also face service-level oversight.
The full AV Act in-use regime is broader but remains part of staged implementation.
sections.takeaway: Current pilot reporting and future AV Act in-use regulation must remain visibly distinct.

sections.title: AEVA 2018 provides the current insurer-first adaptation
paragraphs: Where an insured vehicle is listed as self-driving and causes an accident while driving itself, AEVA 2018 creates a route for insurer liability, subject to statutory conditions.
This does not eliminate product liability, contributory conduct, recovery or other parties' responsibility.
sections.takeaway: The current UK-specific liability innovation is insurer-first treatment for listed self-driving vehicles.

sections.title: The full AV Act framework is targeted for 2027
paragraphs: Government materials state that the broader AV Act framework is expected to operate from the second half of 2027, including authorisation and new responsibility roles.
The draft Statement of Safety Principles consultation remains open until 9 September 2026 and is not Current Law.
sections.takeaway: Show a current pilot route and a future full framework without merging their legal effects.

deploymentConclusion: Great Britain cannot be classified simply as either pilot-only or full deployment law: both descriptions omit part of the current position.
A no-safety-driver pilot and APS route exist in 2026, while the permanent AV Act architecture remains under staged implementation.
Every conclusion must be scoped to Great Britain rather than the whole United Kingdom.
practicalQuestions: Which vehicle approval route and registration steps apply?
Which departures require a VSO, and can the vehicle be listed as self-driving?
Does the service require an APS permit and local consent?
How are ADS capability, cybersecurity, software updating and operations demonstrated?
Which requirements are current pilot duties, and which remain future AV Act law?

terminologyRecords.whyItMatters: It is not the Category 2 operator.

terminologyRecords.explanation: The person performing programme-defined monitoring, routing/dispatch and activation/deactivation functions.
terminologyRecords.whyItMatters: The operator is not a remote driver performing the driving task.

terminologyRecords.explanation: An entity admitted to the EPR and subject to programme duties.
terminologyRecords.whyItMatters: It is not automatically identical to manufacturer, developer, owner or transport operator.

terminologyRecords.explanation: A programme document setting out the VATS safety basis and characteristics.
terminologyRecords.whyItMatters: It does not replace the conformity conclusion or EPR participation.

terminologyRecords.explanation: The accredited laboratory conclusion used in the vehicle-admission process.
terminologyRecords.whyItMatters: It is not general national type approval for unrestricted AV deployment.

terminologyRecords.explanation: The source-native description of environmental and operational conditions for the system.
terminologyRecords.whyItMatters: It may map to the operating-domain question but is not a literal statutory ODD.

terminologyRecords.explanation: The legally relevant territorial scope for operation under the programme.
terminologyRecords.whyItMatters: It is distinct from the ordinary operating environment and from technical ODD.

terminologyRecords.explanation: The mode in which the automated control system performs the driving task.
terminologyRecords.whyItMatters: Keep the term tied to the EPR definition, not a marketing label.

terminologyRecords.englishGloss: statutory test for safe and autonomous travel
terminologyRecords.explanation: The AV Act concept used for future self-driving authorisation.
terminologyRecords.whyItMatters: It belongs to the full AV Act framework, not the current pilot alone.

terminologyRecords.explanation: An order used in the pilot route to address specified legal departures.
terminologyRecords.whyItMatters: A VSO is neither self-driving listing nor an APS permit.

terminologyRecords.englishGloss: listing under the current self-driving/insurance framework
terminologyRecords.explanation: The Secretary of State's list identifying models/variants deemed self-driving.
terminologyRecords.whyItMatters: Listing is not future AV Act authorisation and does not replace the pilot route.

terminologyRecords.explanation: The bespoke permit for passenger services involving automated vehicle technology.
terminologyRecords.whyItMatters: It is separate from vehicle approval, VSO and listing.

terminologyRecords.englishGloss: driver ready to resume control during trials
terminologyRecords.explanation: The human role required for trialling under the code-of-practice route.
terminologyRecords.whyItMatters: The no-safety-driver pilot is legally distinct.

terminologyRecords.englishGloss: future entity responsible for an authorised self-driving feature
terminologyRecords.explanation: A responsibility role created by the Automated Vehicles Act 2024.
terminologyRecords.whyItMatters: Do not present it as the current pilot operator before relevant commencement.

terminologyRecords.englishGloss: in-vehicle user role under the future framework
terminologyRecords.explanation: A person in position to exercise control under the AV Act architecture.
terminologyRecords.whyItMatters: It is not relevant to every no-user-in-charge service.

terminologyRecords.explanation: The future AV Act operator role for operations without a user-in-charge.
terminologyRecords.whyItMatters: Do not use it as the current pilot operator label before commencement.

terminologyRecords.explanation: The statement required by section 2 of the AV Act to guide future authorisation and monitoring.
terminologyRecords.whyItMatters: The September 2026 text is a draft consultation, not current binding criteria.

implementationWatch.title: California CPUC autonomous passenger-service rulemaking
implementationWatch.summary: A successor rulemaking opened in August 2025 to address unresolved AV passenger-service issues. Proposals in that proceeding are not current programme rules.

implementationWatch.title: Draft permanent federal VATS law
implementationWatch.summary: The Ministry of Transport presented a draft intended to move VATS operation from experimental regimes into a permanent public-road framework. It is not current law.

implementationWatch.title: Full Automated Vehicles Act authorisation framework
implementationWatch.summary: The comprehensive authorisation, ASDE, UiC/NUiC and in-use framework is being commenced in stages and is expected to operate more fully from the second half of 2027.

implementationWatch.title: Draft Statement of Safety Principles
implementationWatch.summary: Consultation closes on 9 September 2026. The draft must not be used as current binding authorisation criteria.
